The Bhakti Movement was a major socio religious reform movement in medieval India that emphasized personal devotion to God over ritualism. It emerged in different parts of India between the 7th and 17th centuries and played a crucial role in shaping Indian religious and cultural life.

ORIGIN AND EVOLUTION

• Originated in South India with Alvars and Nayanars between 7th and 9th centuries
• Later spread to North India from 13th century onwards
• Influenced by socio religious conditions including rigid caste system and ritualism
• Encouraged direct devotion without priestly mediation

SOUTH INDIAN TRADITION

• Alvars were Vaishnavite saints devoted to Vishnu
• Nayanars were Shaivite saints devoted to Shiva
• They composed devotional hymns in Tamil
• Strong opposition to caste discrimination and ritualism
• Important in spreading temple based devotional culture

NORTH INDIAN TRADITION

• Emerged from 13th century onwards
• Saints used vernacular languages to reach common people
• Two major streams: Nirguna and Saguna Bhakti

NIRGUNA BHAKTI

• Belief in formless God without attributes
• Rejected idol worship and rituals
• Emphasized inner devotion and equality
• Major saints included Kabir and Guru Nanak

SAGUNA BHAKTI

• Belief in God with form and attributes
• Devotion towards Rama or Krishna
• Emphasized love, surrender and devotion
• Major saints included Tulsidas, Surdas, Mirabai and Chaitanya Mahaprabhu

IMPORTANT SAINTS

• Kabir emphasized unity of God and criticized both Hindu and Muslim orthodoxy
• Guru Nanak founded Sikhism and emphasized equality and devotion
• Tulsidas wrote Ramcharitmanas in Awadhi
• Surdas composed devotional songs on Krishna
• Mirabai was devoted to Krishna and rejected royal life
• Chaitanya promoted ecstatic devotion to Krishna in Bengal

PHILOSOPHICAL BASE

• Emphasis on Bhakti as the path to salvation
• Rejection of caste hierarchy in spiritual matters
• Focus on personal relationship between devotee and God
• Use of simple language and songs for communication

SOCIAL IMPACT

• Challenged caste discrimination and social inequalities
• Promoted equality and social harmony
• Encouraged use of regional languages leading to growth of literature
• Brought religion closer to common people

RELATION WITH SUFI MOVEMENT

• Bhakti and Sufi movements had similarities in emphasis on love and devotion
• Both opposed rigid orthodoxy and rituals
• Encouraged spiritual unity and tolerance

LIMITATIONS

• Did not completely eliminate caste system
• Influence remained limited in some regions
• Social change was gradual rather than revolutionary

SIGNIFICANCE

• Democratized religion by making it accessible to masses
• Strengthened regional languages and literature
• Promoted social reform and religious tolerance
• Left lasting cultural and spiritual legacy in India

IMPORTANT POINTS

• Origin in South India with Alvars and Nayanars
• Two streams: Nirguna and Saguna Bhakti
• Kabir and Nanak associated with Nirguna tradition
• Tulsidas, Surdas and Mirabai associated with Saguna tradition
• Emphasis on devotion over ritualism

PYQ TRAP

UPSC often confuses Nirguna and Saguna Bhakti. Nirguna means formless God and rejects idol worship, while Saguna accepts God with form like Rama or Krishna. Alvars were Vaishnavites and Nayanars were Shaivites.
Medieval History.Sufi Movement:
INTRODUCTION

The Sufi Movement was a mystical dimension of Islam that emphasized love, devotion and direct connection with God. It spread in India from the 12th century onwards and played a significant role in promoting spiritual harmony and cultural synthesis.

ORIGIN AND NATURE

• Originated in West Asia as a mystical tradition within Islam
• Emphasized inner spirituality over formal rituals and orthodoxy
• Focused on love, devotion and unity with God
• Sufis were organized into orders called Silsilah

KEY CONCEPTS

• Tauhid means unity of God
• Zikr refers to remembrance of God through repetition of divine names
• Sama refers to devotional music and singing
• Fana means annihilation of self in God
• Baqa means eternal existence with God

SILSILAHS OR ORDERS

• Chishti order was the most influential in India
• Suhrawardi order had closer relations with the state
• Qadiri and Naqshbandi orders emerged later
• Each Silsilah had its own spiritual practices and lineage

CHISHTI ORDER

• Founded in India by Khwaja Moinuddin Chishti at Ajmer
• Emphasized simplicity, poverty and service to humanity
• Maintained distance from political power
• Important saints include Qutbuddin Bakhtiyar Kaki, Nizamuddin Auliya and Baba Farid
• Use of music and devotional gatherings was common

SUHRAWARDI ORDER

• Founded by Shihabuddin Suhrawardi
• Maintained closer relations with rulers
• Accepted state patronage and official positions
• Important saint in India was Bahauddin Zakariya of Multan

NAQSHBANDI ORDER

• More orthodox and conservative
• Opposed practices like music and sama
• Supported strict adherence to Islamic law
• Associated with Sheikh Ahmad Sirhindi

QADIRI ORDER

• Popular in later medieval period
• Less rigid compared to Naqshbandi
• Spread widely in different parts of India

IMPORTANT SAINTS

• Khwaja Moinuddin Chishti established Chishti order in India
• Nizamuddin Auliya was the most famous Chishti saint in Delhi
• Baba Farid contributed to Punjabi literature and Sikh scriptures
• Sheikh Ahmad Sirhindi was associated with Naqshbandi order

PRACTICES

• Khanqahs were centers of Sufi activity
• Dargahs were tombs of Sufi saints and became pilgrimage centers
• Langar system provided food to followers and poor
• Emphasis on service, charity and equality

SOCIAL IMPACT

• Promoted communal harmony and tolerance
• Attracted followers from different religious backgrounds
• Reduced social divisions and caste barriers
• Encouraged use of local languages and cultural exchange

RELATION WITH STATE

• Chishti saints generally avoided political power
• Suhrawardi saints maintained relations with rulers
• Naqshbandi order supported orthodox policies of rulers like Aurangzeb

SIGNIFICANCE

• Strengthened cultural interaction between Hindu and Muslim communities
• Spread message of love, tolerance and unity
• Influenced Bhakti Movement and vice versa
• Played important role in Indian spiritual traditions

IMPORTANT POINTS

• Sufism emphasizes love and devotion to God
• Organized into Silsilah or orders
• Chishti order most influential in India
• Khanqah is a Sufi center and Dargah is tomb of saint
• Zikr and Sama are important practices

PYQ TRAP

UPSC often confuses Chishti and Suhrawardi orders. Chishtis avoided political power and emphasized simplicity, while Suhrawardis accepted state patronage. Naqshbandi order opposed music and emphasized orthodoxy.
Medieval History.Early Mughals:
INTRODUCTION

The Mughal Empire was one of the most powerful and centralized empires in Indian history. It was founded in 1526 CE and shaped medieval Indian polity, economy, culture, architecture and administration. The Mughal phase is important not only for territorial expansion but also for imperial institutions such as Mansabdari, Jagirdari and revenue administration.

BABUR

• Babur founded the Mughal Empire after defeating Ibrahim Lodi in the First Battle of Panipat in 1526 CE
• He defeated Rana Sanga in the Battle of Khanwa in 1527 CE and Medini Rai in the Battle of Chanderi in 1528 CE
• He used gunpowder, matchlocks and field artillery effectively in Indian warfare
• His memoir Tuzuk i Baburi or Baburnama is an important source
• His rule was short but he laid the military foundation of the empire

HUMAYUN

• Humayun faced constant resistance from Afghan chiefs and internal family rivalries
• He lost the empire to Sher Shah Suri after defeats at Chausa in 1539 CE and Kannauj in 1540 CE
• He spent years in exile and later regained the throne with Persian support in 1555 CE
• His reign is important because it shows the fragility of the early Mughal state

AKBAR

• Akbar was the real consolidator of the Mughal Empire
• He defeated Hemu in the Second Battle of Panipat in 1556 CE
• He expanded Mughal authority over North India, Gujarat, Bengal, Kashmir and parts of Deccan
• He abolished jizya for a period and followed Sulh i kul or universal peace
• He developed a strong centralized administration and brought Rajputs into imperial service
• His court historian Abul Fazl wrote Akbarnama and Ain i Akbari

ADMINISTRATION UNDER AKBAR

• The empire was divided into Suba, Sarkar, Pargana and village
• The emperor was supreme authority at the center
• Major central officers included Wazir, Mir Bakshi, Sadr us Sudur and Qazi
• Provincial administration was headed by Subahdar with separate financial and military officers
• This separation reduced concentration of power in one office

MANSABDARI SYSTEM

• Mansabdari system was introduced by Akbar
• Mansab meant rank and position in the imperial hierarchy
• Zat indicated personal status and salary
• Sawar indicated the number of cavalry to be maintained
• Mansabdars were appointed, promoted and transferred by the emperor
• This system combined civil and military service in one imperial framework

JAGIRDARI SYSTEM

• Jagir was a revenue assignment given to Mansabdars in place of cash salary
• Jagirdars did not own land permanently
• They were entitled to collect revenue from assigned areas on behalf of the state
• Frequent transfer of Jagirs was intended to prevent local power buildup
• In the later Mughal phase, Jagirdari crisis became an important factor in imperial decline

REVENUE SYSTEM

• Akbar's revenue administration was systematized under Raja Todar Mal
• Zabti system was based on measurement of land and assessment of average produce and prices
• Land was classified according to cultivation and productivity
• Dahsala system used ten year average for revenue assessment
• Revenue administration strengthened imperial finances and agrarian control

JAHANGIR

• Jahangir maintained the imperial structure built by Akbar
• He is associated with the chain of justice as a symbol of royal accessibility
• His reign saw the growing political influence of Nur Jahan
• Mughal painting reached refinement during his time, especially naturalistic studies of birds, animals and flowers
• English East India Company received permission to trade during this period

SHAH JAHAN

• Shah Jahan's reign is regarded as the period of Mughal architectural zenith
• He built the Taj Mahal, Red Fort of Delhi and Jama Masjid
• Imperial grandeur and court ceremonial reached high refinement
• Military campaigns continued in the Deccan and Central Asia frontier zones
• Heavy expenditure on architecture and warfare increased fiscal pressure

AURANGZEB

• Aurangzeb expanded the Mughal Empire to its maximum territorial extent
• He annexed Bijapur and Golconda and pursued long Deccan campaigns
• He reimposed jizya and followed a more orthodox religious policy than Akbar
• His reign faced revolts from Marathas, Jats, Sikhs and Satnamis
• Continuous warfare overextended the empire and weakened central control
• His period marks both territorial expansion and the beginning of serious imperial strain

ECONOMY

• Agriculture was the backbone of Mughal economy
• India produced wheat, rice, sugarcane, cotton and indigo on a large scale
• Textile production was highly developed and Indian textiles were in demand in world markets
• Urban centers such as Agra, Lahore, Delhi and Ahmedabad flourished
• Inland and overseas trade expanded under imperial stability

RELIGION AND IDEAS

• Akbar followed Sulh i kul based on tolerance and peace among all communities
• He discontinued pilgrimage tax and attempted to reduce religious discrimination
• Din i Ilahi was a small ethical order associated with Akbar and not a mass religion
• Aurangzeb's reign reflected greater orthodoxy and closer association with Islamic law

ART AND ARCHITECTURE

• Mughal architecture combined Persian, Central Asian and Indian elements
• Humayun's Tomb represents an early major example of Mughal architecture in India
• Fatehpur Sikri reflects Akbar's architectural vision
• Taj Mahal represents the peak of Mughal funerary architecture
• Mughal painting developed under Akbar, Jahangir and Shah Jahan
• Gardens, forts, mosques and mausoleums were major architectural forms

LITERATURE AND SOURCES

• Baburnama is an autobiographical source for Babur
• Akbarnama and Ain i Akbari by Abul Fazl are crucial for Akbar's reign
• Tuzuk i Jahangiri is an important source for Jahangir
• Court chronicles provide details of administration, economy and imperial ideology

DECLINE

• Weak successors after Aurangzeb could not maintain strong central authority
• Jagirdari crisis, factional struggles and financial pressure weakened the empire
• Regional powers such as Marathas, Sikhs, Jats and later autonomous Nawabs rose in strength
• Repeated invasions and internal fragmentation accelerated decline in the 18th century

SIGNIFICANCE

The Mughal Empire gave India a durable imperial framework, a sophisticated administrative structure, a major tradition of architecture and painting, and a powerful legacy in agrarian and revenue organization. Its institutions influenced later regional states and even colonial administration.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• Babur founded the empire in 1526 CE after the First Battle of Panipat
• Akbar was the real consolidator of Mughal rule
• Mansabdari was a rank system and Jagir was a revenue assignment
• Zabti and Dahsala are associated with Mughal revenue administration
• Jahangir is known for chain of justice and refined painting
• Shah Jahan is associated with architectural grandeur
• Aurangzeb expanded the empire most but also intensified strains of decline

PYQ TRAP

UPSC often confuses Mansab and Jagir. Mansab means rank while Jagir means revenue assignment. Sulh i kul is associated with Akbar, not Aurangzeb. Din i Ilahi was not a mass religion. Zabti is a revenue system, not a military arrangement.
Medieval History.Early Marathas:
INTRODUCTION

The rise of the Marathas in the 17th century marked a significant shift in Indian political history. Under Shivaji, the Marathas established a strong regional power that later challenged Mughal dominance and laid the foundation for a pan Indian empire.

BACKGROUND

• Decline of Deccan Sultanates and weakening of Mughal control in Deccan
• Harsh Mughal policies under Aurangzeb created resentment
• Geographical conditions of Western Ghats favored guerrilla warfare
• Rise of local warrior groups and leadership under Shivaji

SHIVAJI

• Founder of Maratha power
• Born in 1630 CE at Shivneri Fort
• Son of Shahji Bhonsle and Jijabai
• Influenced by Bhakti saints and regional traditions
• Established independent kingdom through military skill and diplomacy

MILITARY SYSTEM

• Followed guerrilla warfare known as Ganimi Kava
• Strong network of forts for defense and control
• Efficient cavalry and light infantry
• Avoided large scale open battles
• Developed a navy to protect western coast

ADMINISTRATION

• Established a centralized administration
• Introduced Ashtapradhan council of eight ministers
• Key positions included Peshwa, Amatya, Sachiv, Senapati and others
• Efficient system of governance and record keeping

REVENUE SYSTEM

• Chauth was one fourth of revenue collected from territories
• Sardeshmukhi was an additional ten percent tax
• Land revenue formed main source of income
• Revenue collection was systematic and supervised

RELIGIOUS POLICY

• Followed policy of tolerance towards all religions
• Protected temples and respected local traditions
• Avoided unnecessary religious conflicts

EXPANSION

• Captured territories from Bijapur and Mughals
• Established control over large parts of Maharashtra
• Raids into Mughal territories weakened their control

SUCCESSORS

• Sambhaji succeeded Shivaji but faced Mughal opposition
• Rajaram continued resistance from southern forts
• Tarabai played important role in sustaining Maratha resistance

SIGNIFICANCE

• Established Maratha power as major political force
• Introduced effective military and administrative systems
• Laid foundation for later Maratha expansion across India
• Challenged Mughal supremacy in Deccan

IMPORTANT POINTS

• Shivaji is founder of Maratha power
• Ashtapradhan was council of ministers
• Guerrilla warfare was key military strategy
• Chauth and Sardeshmukhi were major taxes
• Forts played crucial role in defense

PYQ TRAP

UPSC often confuses Maratha revenue terms. Chauth was one fourth tax while Sardeshmukhi was an additional ten percent. Ashtapradhan was administrative council under Shivaji, not under Peshwas.

ADVENT OF EUROPEANS IN INDIA

Introduction
• The advent of Europeans in India marked the beginning of a new phase in Indian history, eventually leading to colonial domination.
• The primary objective of Europeans was trade, especially in spices, textiles and luxury goods.
• Over time, commercial interests transformed into political and territorial control.

Background
• Renaissance in Europe increased curiosity and scientific temperament.
• Fall of Constantinople (1453) blocked traditional land trade routes to Asia.
• Rise of Mercantilism encouraged accumulation of bullion through trade.
• Need to bypass Arab intermediaries and Ottoman control.
• Advances in navigation (compass, astrolabe, cartography, shipbuilding).

PORTUGUESE

Introduction
• First Europeans to arrive in India.
• Vasco da Gama reached Calicut in 1498.

Important Points
• Established first factory at Calicut.
• Followed policy of trade monopoly and naval dominance.
• Introduced Cartaz system (naval passes for trade).

Key Governors
• Francisco de Almeida – First Governor, followed ‘Blue Water Policy’ (naval supremacy).
• Alfonso de Albuquerque – Real founder of Portuguese power in India.

Features
• Captured Goa (1510) → became headquarters.
• Captured Malacca and Hormuz → control of trade routes.
• Introduced Christianity through missionaries.

Decline
• Weak successors after Albuquerque.
• Corruption and mismanagement.
• Rise of Dutch and English competition.
• Loss of naval supremacy.

PYQ Trap
• Blue Water Policy = Almeida (not Albuquerque).
• Goa captured in 1510 (frequently asked).

DUTCH

Introduction
• Dutch East India Company (VOC) established in 1602.

Important Points
• Focused mainly on spice trade (Indonesia priority).
• Established factories at Masulipatnam, Pulicat, Nagapattinam.

Features
• Strong naval power.
• Monopoly over spice trade in East Indies.

Decline
• Defeated by English in Battle of Bedara (1759).
• Shifted focus to Indonesia.

PYQ Trap
• Dutch decline in India due to English defeat, not Indian resistance.

ENGLISH

Introduction
• English East India Company established in 1600.
• Arrived for trade but later became political rulers.

Important Points
• First factory at Surat (1613).
• Sir Thomas Roe secured trade privileges from Jahangir.

Expansion
• Madras (Fort St George) – 1639
• Bombay – acquired from Portuguese (1661)
• Calcutta (Fort William) – 1690

Features
• Shift from trade to territorial control.
• Strong naval supremacy.
• Use of diplomacy and military power.

Significance
• Gradually emerged as dominant European power.
• Laid foundation of British Empire in India.

PYQ Trap
• First factory → Surat (not Madras).
• Bombay came from Portuguese dowry (Catherine of Braganza).

FRENCH

Introduction
• French East India Company established in 1664.

Important Points
• Main centres: Pondicherry, Chandernagore, Mahe, Karaikal.

Features
• Strong political ambitions under Dupleix.
• Direct rivalry with English.

Carnatic Wars
• First Carnatic War (1746–48)
• Second Carnatic War (1749–54)
• Third Carnatic War (1758–63)

Outcome
• English victory → French political influence ended.

PYQ Trap
• Dupleix associated with French expansion.
• Carnatic Wars decided British supremacy.

DANISH

Introduction
• Danish East India Company established in 1616.

Important Points
• Settlements at Tranquebar and Serampore.

Features
• Limited political role.
• Focused mainly on trade and missionary activities.

Decline
• Sold settlements to British in 19th century.

COMPARATIVE ANALYSIS

Important Points
• Portuguese – First arrivals, early dominance.
• Dutch – Trade focused, lost to English.
• French – Political challenge, lost in Carnatic Wars.
• English – Most successful, established empire.

Significance

• Beginning of European colonialism in India.
• Integration of Indian economy with global trade.
• Shift from trade to territorial imperialism.
• Foundation of British rule.

PYQ Trap
• Sequence: Portuguese → Dutch → English → French → Danish.
• Only English succeeded in long-term political control.

Conclusion
• The advent of Europeans transformed India’s political and economic structure.
• What started as trade eventually resulted in colonial rule, with long-term consequences for India.
